title: Fit a circlip into the groove of a loose shaft with circlip pliers: spread it just enough, seat it, turn it to check
instruction: Fit the retaining ring into the groove on the shaft with the circlip pliers, then put the pliers down.
context: Industrial machinery mechanics, machinery maintenance workers and millwrights (about 547,300 US jobs in 2025, BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook) repair or replace machine parts as a core duty, and refitting the external retaining ring, or circlip, that keeps a gear or bearing on its shaft is part of that work. A shaft this size (40 mm, 1.6 kg) is worked loose on the bench: the fitter stands it on end, steadies it with one hand and works the pliers with the other. The ring is spread in its two lug holes only as far as it takes to pass over the shaft, slid to its groove, let close into it, then turned to check it is seated all round. Ring makers give a maximum installation spread because spring steel opened past it takes a permanent set and sits loose in its groove. A ring let go short of the groove grips the shaft in the wrong place, and one let go tilted lands half in the groove.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0. A loose shaft assembly stands on end on the bench with its axis at x 36, y -6. Nothing clamps or fixes it: it can slide, turn or be knocked over. It is a ground steel shaft 40 mm in diameter and 14.9 cm long, standing on its lower end (1 mm chamfer), with a 46 mm shoulder from z 8.8 to 9.4 and a steel spur gear (56 mm across, 30 teeth, 1.6 cm thick) sitting on the shoulder from z 9.4 to 11.0. The assembly weighs about 1.6 kg. Below the shoulder the shaft is plain, which is where a hand holds it. Just above the gear the shaft has a retaining-ring groove 1.85 mm wide with a 37.5 mm bottom diameter (DIN 471 for 40 mm), its lower wall flush with the gear's top face, from z 11.0 to 11.19. The end face is at z 14.9 with a 1.5 mm chamfer. The ring is a DIN 471 external retaining ring for a 40 mm shaft, spring steel with a bright yellow zinc-chromate plating, 1.75 mm thick, 4.5 mm wide, free bore 36.5 mm, with two lug holes 12 mm apart; it lies flat on the shaft's end face, lugs toward the robot (at x 33.6). Its bore grows by (lug spacing - 12 mm) / pi: it clears the shaft from 40.2 mm (lug spacing 23.6 mm). Closed in its groove the ring grips the groove bottom with about 270 N, so turning it there takes about 0.61 N·m, and that torque turns the shaft too unless the shaft is held (both figures are estimates; see fidelity). Spread clear of the shaft, it pushes nothing on it. The circlip pliers are external pliers with 90-degree bent tips, 13 cm long and 130 g: red handle grips 8 x 1.0 x 1.2 cm, 4.0 cm apart outside at rest; steel jaws crossing at a rivet; tips 1.7 cm long and 2.6 mm thick, 12 mm apart at rest. Squeezing the handles 1 mm closer spreads the tips 1 mm, up to an 18 mm stop. They lie along x on a black rubber rest block (8 x 3 x 3 cm, centered x 25.6, y -22), handles on the block with the grip point at x 26.1, y -22, z 3.6, tips toward +x hanging past the block's end at x 33.6.
scoring: The score is the ring's state at the end of the run, after two damage checks kept over the whole run. Doing nothing scores 0. Over-spread: 0, irreversible, if the ring's bore ever exceeded 41.0 mm (lug spacing 26.1 mm), 1 mm (2.5%) over the shaft, the usual maximum installation spread for this ring, because spring steel opened further takes a set and sits loose in the groove, where it can walk out under load. The sim computes that set from the spread; a real trial measures it: the largest lug spacing on the top video against a mm scale, and the ring's free bore with calipers after it is taken off (over 36.6 mm, against 36.5 mm new, means a set). Bent: 0 if the ring's ends were twisted more than 10 degrees out of its plane (2.1 mm across the 12 mm lug spacing) for two control steps in a row, so a one-step jolt of the pliers does not count. The sim treats that twist as a bent ring, a modeled stand-in; a real trial lays the removed ring on a flat plate and fails it if a 0.1 mm feeler gauge slides under any part. Otherwise the score climbs with real progress. 0.25: the ring is on the shaft, its mid-plane at least 5 mm past the end face (clear of the 1.5 mm chamfer; a ruler from the end face in a real trial), but not seated: short of the groove, cocked or held open by the pliers. Getting a ring over the shaft end without over-spreading it is the controlled-spread part of the job, and a ring left there can be spread again and moved, so it is worth a quarter. 0.5: seated, meaning in the groove, closed onto its 37.5 mm bottom and not cocked. The pliers' tips may still be in the lug holes; a ring they hold open is not closed. A ring closed into the groove while tilted more than 4 degrees is cocked: its far side sits 3.4 mm off the groove plane, nearly twice the 1.85 mm groove width, so it lands on the shaft beside the groove and is not seated. Seated, the ring does its job, so it is worth half. 0.75: seated and turned at least 15 degrees net in its groove (5 mm at its rim), the fitter's check that it is free all round and not caught on the shaft. Net means the span between the smallest and largest angle it reached there, so wiggling back and forth counts only the wiggle's width. The turn counts on the shaft: the ring grips the shaft, so a shaft left free turns with the pliers and the ring does not turn on it, and that is no check. 1.0: that, plus the work put down. The pliers are out of the ring, no gripper touches them (contact with the hand's own shape, within 2 mm), and they lie still on the bench or the rest (grip point from 1 cm below to 5 cm above the bench top, over its footprint, not on the floor or left on the shaft). The job is not finished while the tool is still in hand or hanging off the work. The shaft must also be standing on its end on the bench (axis within 10 degrees of vertical, lower end within 1 cm of the bench top), not knocked over or off the bench, where a loose 1.6 kg part can roll and fall. How the shaft is steadied is up to the robot, and where the arms end up is not scored. A real trial also checks seating with a straightedge on the gear face at four points and the turn with a paint mark on the ring against one on the shaft.
reset_notes: Take the ring off with the pliers (spread no more than 41 mm), check its free bore with calipers and that it lies flat on a plate, and replace it if the bore measures over 36.6 mm or a 0.1 mm feeler gauge slides under it. Lay it on the shaft's end face with the lugs toward the robot, stand the shaft assembly on end at its marked spot, and put the pliers back on the rest block.
fidelity: The ring is a model driven by the pliers' tips in its lug holes, with DIN 471 sizes. Closed on the shaft it grips it (about 270 N, estimated from the maker's 14,000 rpm detaching speed), so turning it puts up to 0.61 N·m (mu 0.12, estimated) on the shaft, which turns with it unless held. Spread clear of the shaft, it pushes nothing on it. The pliers feel no reaction and the ring no sideways push. The shaft, pliers and hands are real bodies; the jaws are a 1:1 crossed slide.
